Session 4 Facilitator Rehearsal Run Sheet

Make the choice survivable

Version: 2026-08-23 Format: 135-minute live cohort session Cohort: up to 10 PMs with approximately 2-6 years of experience Deck: 19-page HTML/PDF facilitator deck Preparation: the Session 4 pre-read is not released in the current site build; do not treat the live deck as its substitute

This is a rehearsal document, not a teleprompter. It is intentionally fuller than the spoken delivery. Rehearse the argument, case logic, questions, transitions, and recovery language; then teach in your own voice.

The facilitator's job

By the end of the session, learners should be able to carry a product decision through commitment, changing execution conditions, and observed outcomes without confusing:

  1. participation with decision authority;
  2. alignment with unanimous preference;
  3. product confidence with engineering effort confidence;
  4. adaptation with PM takeover;
  5. deployment with exposure, outcome, or durable impact; and
  6. outcome quality with decision quality.

The governing message is:

The PM remains accountable after the choice: make ownership portable, adapt the system around the work, contain exposure, and review the original reasoning honestly.

Session 3 ended with a strategic direction, portfolio, sequence, technical option, thresholds, and owners. Session 4 does not add a new strategy. It tests whether the choice can survive contact with people, delivery, and outcome.

Source and accuracy stance

  • The required teaching spine is Reforge-derived and reorganized into the course's own decision-survival loop.
  • The Noted product is real; Week 4 stakeholders, dependencies, estimates, exposure counts, outcomes, and operating-system failures are constructed for practice.WN-04
  • Commitment is treated as shared understanding and obligation, not consensus or persuasion theater.S4-SN-03S4-SN-04
  • Product and engineering confidence remain distinct. Product cannot promise feasibility on engineering's behalf.S4-SN-06
  • Product review is input and resolution, not general oversight. Temporary intervention must have a return-to-autonomy condition.S4-SN-09S4-SN-10
  • Production impact can differ from test impact because population, implementation, novelty, pull-forward, confounding, and operating context change.S4-SN-14
  • The outcome numbers are illustrative. They test interpretation, ownership, and learning discipline—not statistical calculation.

For a 150-minute version, add five minutes to each debrief. Do not add project-management or release-tool instruction.

Before learners arrive

  • Open the HTML deck and verify arrow-key navigation and fullscreen mode.
  • Keep a visible six-minute timer ready for slides 8, 13, and 17.
  • Prepare one capture surface with seven headings: owner, participation, dissent, ask, intervention, exposure, and system change.
  • Keep the Week 3 Strategy and Constraint Choice visible. Do not allow Week 4 difficulties to silently reopen the strategic direction.
  • Ask learners to keep each answer private until the timer ends. Select two or three responses yourself; there is no peer-discussion requirement.
  • Treat every Week 4 event and number as constructed.WN-04
  • Reserve the last six minutes for open Q&A, but redirect requests for a generic stakeholder-management workshop, sprint process, or release tooling.

Facilitation stance

Use five moves throughout:

  1. Differentiate participation. Ask: "Does this person need awareness, input, alignment, or authority?"
  2. Keep confidence honest. Ask: "What does product know, and what must engineering validate?"
  3. Adapt the system first. Ask: "Can sequence, interface, review, exposure, or scope change before ownership changes?"
  4. Make intervention temporary. Ask: "What condition returns control to the original owner?"
  5. Reconstruct before judging. Ask: "What was known, forecast, and chosen at the time?"

Useful recovery phrases:

  • "Disagreement can remain after commitment. Who owns the call?"
  • "What exact input or decision do you need from this stakeholder?"
  • "Product conviction is not an engineering estimate."
  • "You have changed the plan. Have you also changed the strategy, or only the execution path?"
  • "What interface is unclear enough to create the takeover pressure?"
  • "Deployed does not tell us who was exposed."
  • "A favorable outcome does not repair a weak decision process."
  • "What will the team do differently next time because of this review?"

Avoid these phrases:

  • "We need everybody's buy-in."
  • "The stakeholder was consulted, so they co-own the decision."
  • "Engineering will figure it out" when confidence is materially low.
  • "I'll just take it over to unblock the team."
  • "More meetings will fix the alignment."
  • "We launched, so now we can measure impact."
  • "The result proves the strategy worked."
  • "In hindsight, we should obviously have known."

Slide-by-slide rehearsal script

Slide 1 - Make the choice survivable

Time: 4 minutes Job: Position commitment, adaptation, and learning as Core PM work after strategy.

Rehearse

"The roadmap is not where product accountability ends. A defensible decision can still fail because people do not know their rights, execution changes silently, exposure outruns control, or the team rewrites the story after the result."
"Today we make the choice survivable. First, create commitment without demanding consensus. Second, adapt execution without taking ownership back. Third, learn from the outcome without turning hindsight into a verdict on what was knowable."
"This is not a generic leadership session. Every people and delivery move exists to preserve the quality, ownership, and learning of the product decision."

Ask

"Which is more common in your environment: a decision that never becomes commitment, or a commitment that disappears as soon as execution changes?"

Do not collect a full round.

Transition

"We will follow the same decision through four states."

Slide 2 - The decision-survival loop

Time: 6 minutes Job: Establish the cumulative logic and the Week 4 capstone outcome.

Rehearse

"Commitment makes context, authority, confidence, dissent, and asks explicit. Adaptation changes sequence, interfaces, review depth, and intervention as reality becomes clearer. Exposure contains consequence and preserves reversibility. Learning compares the original forecast with the outcome and changes both the product decision and the operating system."
"The loop is not cleanly linear. Low engineering confidence can narrow commitment. A new dependency can change exposure. An instrumentation gap can prevent learning and force another bounded cycle."
"The Week 4 output completes the Product Decision Case. It is not a shipping retrospective. A learner without a launched product can still state a prospective exposure plan, decision rule, attribution boundary, and system-learning trigger."

Transition

"Here are the three Week 4 pressures on the Noted choice."

Slide 3 - Noted Week 4 consequence release

Time: 6 minutes Job: Introduce people, delivery, and outcome tensions without resolving them.

Rehearse

"The strategic direction is enterprise decision handoff. Sales still believes broad summary intelligence will create pipeline faster. This is legitimate dissent, but the record does not yet show how it is retained or who finally owns the call."
"The permission estimate doubles from two to four weeks because workspace identity depends on an external provider. The PM is tempted to write the detailed plan and coordinate every interface."
"A staged exposure later shows a three-point increase in confirmed follow-through, below the eight-point forecast. One workspace is positive; the other is blocked by governance; 12 percent of actors are unobserved."
"The governing question is what Noted should preserve, change, and learn without dissolving ownership or rewriting the original choice."

Ask

"Which pressure is most likely to cause a PM to overreact: dissent, the estimate change, or the mixed outcome? What form would the overreaction take?"

Take two quick responses.

Transition

"Commitment begins with context people can use."

Slide 4 - Portable context

Time: 5 minutes Job: Distinguish empowering context from implementation prescription.

Rehearse

"Reforge's empowering-spec argument asks PMs to invest more in critical context and decide less of the nonessential implementation. The context includes opportunity, audience, customer and competitive insight, and success metrics.S4-SN-01"
"For Noted: the opportunity is trusted ownership handoff; the audience is team leads in recurring decision-heavy meetings; success is improved follow-through without weakened trust or governance; the exposure and instrumentation boundaries are explicit."
"The PM should not prescribe the internal permission architecture. Engineering needs the context to make an implementation choice that respects product value and risk. More detail is not automatically more empowering. Detail becomes harmful when it silently transfers decisions away from the rightful owner."

Misconception recovery

If a learner asks for every edge case before commitment:

"Which edge case changes the product boundary or risk threshold, and which belongs to the implementation owner?"

Transition

"Context enables action. Participation and authority determine who shapes and who decides."

Slide 5 - Participation and decision rights

Time: 5 minutes Job: Prevent inclusion from becoming ambiguous co-decision.

Rehearse

"Reforge distinguishes awareness, alignment, and inclusion in stakeholder work.S4-SN-03 The course makes the decision right even more explicit: awareness, input, alignment, shaping work, and final authority are different jobs."
"Support, GTM, and Finance need awareness. Sales, Security, and Customer Success provide critical input and alignment. Engineering, Design, and Data shape the work. The product lead owns the product-direction decision."
"Authority is decision-specific, not a single hierarchy for the whole initiative. Product owns the direction, target audience, value threshold, and scope trade-off. Security still owns whether the exposure satisfies the required control boundary; Engineering owns architecture and implementation. Slide 11 will make those domain rights explicit."
"Reforge's opinionated decision-making argument warns that consensus can over-compromise the product and ship the organization chart to the customer.S4-SN-04 Inclusion improves the decision. It does not remove the need for an accountable choice after dissent."
"Sales dissent remains in the record with its evidence and reopening trigger. Alignment means Sales understands the choice and next obligation. It does not mean Sales now prefers it."

Ask

"Where in your current work is input being mistaken for veto power—or awareness being mistaken for required approval?"

Transition

"Even a well-owned product direction cannot commit beyond the team's technical confidence."

Slide 6 - Product and engineering confidence

Time: 4 minutes Job: Separate opportunity conviction from delivery confidence.

Rehearse

"Reforge's Product Conviction material separates confidence in customer value and impact from confidence in effort and alignment. Engineering leaders help identify feasibility, effort, risk, and key challenges.S4-SN-06"
"Noted has enough product confidence to stage: the problem and segment are bounded, the mechanism is plausible, and production impact remains uncertain. Engineering confidence is low on permissions: the identity dependency is unresolved and the estimate range doubled."
"The correct commitment is therefore smaller. Commit to manual workflow and shadow-mode learning. Do not commit to broad rollout or a fixed date. Product confidence cannot compensate for missing engineering understanding."

Transition

"When the organization must resolve the boundary, make the ask exact."

Slide 7 - Preserve dissent and make the ask exact

Time: 4 minutes Job: Turn escalation into an actionable organizational decision.

Rehearse

"Reforge's clear-asks guidance argues that leaders should help executives help them: name what decision, input, resource, or support is required rather than minimizing or obscuring the ask.S4-SN-05"
"The decision remains enterprise handoff. Sales dissent remains visible and can reopen the direction if distribution or enterprise access blocks learning. The exact executive ask is a choice: add identity-platform support for two weeks, or narrow the pilot to manual provisioning."
"The ask has an owner, deadline, and consequence. Without a decision by Tuesday, there is no credible enterprise exposure this cycle. The team should not absorb missing authority as an invisible commitment."

Misconception recovery

If a learner says "leadership support":

"What action must which leader take by when, and what happens if they do not?"

Transition

"Now create the commitment boundary."

Slide 8 - Unit 10 individual decision

Time: 14 minutes total: 6 decide, 8 debrief Job: Observe whether learners create commitment without consensus or false confidence.

Set up the decision

"Define the decision owner, stakeholder participation levels, product confidence, engineering confidence, and unresolved dissent. Then make one exact escalation ask with an owner, deadline, and consequence of no decision."

Model debrief

"The product lead owns the product direction. Engineering, Design, Data, and Security shape the work, and domain owners retain authority for decisions inside their remit. Sales provides input and aligns to the execution obligation but retains its documented disagreement. Support, Finance, and GTM receive the context necessary for awareness and action."
"Product confidence supports a bounded pilot. Engineering confidence does not support broad enterprise provisioning. I ask the CTO to choose by Tuesday between two weeks of identity-platform support and a manual-provisioning pilot. No decision means the rollout remains paused."

What strong judgment sounds like

  • Participation differs by actual decision job.
  • One accountable owner remains visible.
  • Dissent is retained with evidence and a reopening trigger.
  • Product and engineering confidence are stated separately.
  • The ask is exact and consequential.

Weak-answer recovery

If everyone is listed as a decision-maker:

"When the group still disagrees on Tuesday, whose call is it?"

Transition

"Commitment is now bounded. Delivery will immediately make parts of the plan wrong."

Slide 9 - Delivery as a system

Time: 5 minutes Job: Move from ticket progress to confidence, planning, adaptation, and exposure.

Rehearse

"Reforge's delivery system spans conviction, dynamic planning, execution and adaptation, and launch. The durable point is that delivery quality is produced by an interdependent operating system, not by moving tickets faster.S4-SN-02"
"Confidence defines what is known. The plan represents milestones, dependencies, interfaces, and owners. Adaptation changes the system as evidence and effort become clearer. Exposure contains consequence."
"The common failure is that uncertainty creates takeover pressure. The PM writes the plan, resolves every interface, attends every review, and becomes the integration owner. Short-term movement can improve while team ownership collapses."

Ask

"Which part of your delivery system usually changes too late: confidence, sequence, interfaces, review, or exposure?"

Transition

"Start with sequence."

Slide 10 - Re-sequence the dependency

Time: 5 minutes Job: Preserve strategic direction while changing the delivery commitment.

Rehearse

"Reforge's dynamic-planning material begins from the reality that high-level estimates assume optimal conditions and unknown complications emerge during the work. Teams then face conflict because the date or budget was already committed.S4-SN-07"
"The original Noted plan put permissions before intelligence and a two-partner pilot. After the estimate doubles, the revised plan manually provisions Partner A, develops handoff intelligence in shadow mode, and runs an identity spike while Partner B remains on hold."
"The enterprise-handoff direction is stable. The broad provisioning commitment and fixed timing change. This is disciplined adaptation, not strategy drift. The new order preserves product learning while the dependency is resolved."

Misconception recovery

If a learner insists on the original date:

"Which quality, risk, scope, or ownership consequence are you choosing to absorb—and who accepted it?"

Transition

"Sequence alone will not hold if the interfaces and decision rights remain implicit."

Slide 11 - Delegation contract and interfaces

Time: 4 minutes Job: Make delegation compatible with collaboration and integration.

Rehearse

"Reforge's delegate-and-manage material makes work packages, dependencies, and milestones visible.S4-SN-08 Our course position adds a compact contract: owned outcome, decision right, interface and dependency, and integration check."
"Engineering owns a safe workspace-access path and its architecture. Product owns the bounded pilot decision, target value, and scope trade-off. Security owns control approval or an explicit block. Customer Success owns partner readiness and recovery."
"The PM resolves the product trade-off and interface ambiguity. The PM does not absorb architecture, security approval, or onboarding execution. Delegation is not isolation; each integration point remains visible."

Ask

"Which row becomes ambiguous if the phrase 'the team owns it' is the only ownership statement?"

Transition

"Now choose how much review and intervention the consequence requires."

Slide 12 - Proportionate review and temporary intervention

Time: 4 minutes Job: Separate useful product input from oversight and permanent micromanagement.

Rehearse

"Reforge describes product reviews as input, not oversight. Reviews can provide feedback, make a decision, resolve a question, or build awareness, but purpose and stakeholders should be explicit.S4-SN-09 Team touchpoints should respond to coordination need rather than become fixed status theater.S4-SN-10"
"Low consequence needs an async update. Coordination risk triggers a focused review. Material exposure can justify temporarily tighter controls and a stop rule. An unresolved authority or safety boundary requires pause or escalation."
"Selective intervention is defensible only if it is proportional and temporary where possible. For Noted, autonomy returns when the identity path is validated, interfaces have owners, the stop rule is operational, and two reviews close without material surprise."

Transition

"Now adapt the system without taking the work back."

Slide 13 - Unit 11 individual decision

Time: 14 minutes total: 6 decide, 8 debrief Job: Test whether learners can reduce consequence while preserving ownership integrity.

Set up the decision

"Re-sequence the dependency. Define the critical interfaces and decision rights. Choose a proportionate review cadence. Name the stop or escalation condition, temporary intervention, and exact condition for returning autonomy."

Model debrief

"I keep the enterprise-handoff strategy. I manually provision Partner A, run intelligence in shadow mode, and separate the identity spike from the pilot-learning path. Partner B remains paused."
"Engineering owns architecture and the spike; Security owns the control boundary; Product owns scope and value threshold; Customer Success owns partner readiness. We add twice-weekly focused dependency reviews until the identity path is validated."
"We pause if deletion or access controls fail, if actor identity remains materially unobservable, or if the partner cannot operate the recovery path. We return to normal team cadence after two reviews close without material surprise and all interfaces have named owners."

What strong judgment sounds like

  • Strategy and execution changes are separated.
  • Sequence continues learning without hiding the dependency.
  • Interfaces and decision rights are explicit.
  • Review intensity follows consequence.
  • Intervention has an end condition.

Weak-answer recovery

If the PM becomes the plan owner:

"Which missing interface or decision right created the need for takeover? Repair that boundary first."

Transition to break

"Take eight minutes. When we return, the capability has been deployed and exposed—but those words do not yet tell us what happened."

Slide 14 - Deployment, exposure, outcome, and impact

Time: 6 minutes Job: Establish four distinct states before interpreting the result.

Rehearse

"Reforge describes launch as a false finish line and advocates staging strategies that control rollout and preserve the ability to respond.S4-SN-11 Metrics and instrumentation must be prepared before launch so the team can understand post-launch behavior and operate safely.S4-SN-12"
"Deployed means the capability exists in production. Exposed means an eligible population could encounter it. Observed means a measured change appeared. Impact is the durable product and business consequence."
"Noted deployed the capability. Sixty-four eligible meetings across two workspaces could use it, although governance blocked normal use in one. Confirmed follow-through increased by three points, with 12 percent actor missingness. Durable value, retention, trust, and economics remain unknown."
"Do not skip states. If you say 'we launched to two customers,' ask whether the target users and meetings were actually exposed under comparable conditions."

Transition

"Now compare the observed evidence with the rule written before the result."

Slide 15 - Forecast versus result

Time: 7 minutes Job: Update the decision without smoothing population, implementation, or observability differences.

Rehearse

"The pre-decision forecast was an eight-point increase. The expansion rule required clearing five points with no trust guardrail decline. It assumed two enterprise workspaces, known actor and meeting type, and a stable permission path."
"The observed overall change is three points. Partner A is positive at nine; Partner B is negative at one point below baseline after governance blocks normal use. There are only 64 eligible meetings, 12 percent of actors are missing, and implementation differs by workspace."
"Reforge's productizing-wins material warns that test impact and actual production impact can differ because implementation, population, novelty, pull-forward, confounding, and other conditions change.S4-SN-14"
"The justified update is not expand and not declare failure. Continue Partner A, pause Partner B, repair access and observability, then test whether the mechanism transfers. The mixed result has changed the next action even though it has not resolved the strategy."

Misconception recovery

If a learner averages the two partners and concludes no value:

"What population and implementation difference could explain the average, and which transfer claim remains untested?"

Transition

"Before judging the original decision, separate its quality from the outcome."

Slide 16 - Decision quality, outcome quality, and luck

Time: 6 minutes Job: Prevent hindsight from rewarding weak reasoning or punishing defensible uncertainty.

Rehearse

"Reforge's decision-loop and post-mortem materials emphasize review and reflection as a way to build product intuition, not merely report progress.S4-SN-15 The course separates the quality of the reasoning from the quality of the outcome."
"Defensible reasoning with a favorable outcome is earned progress, but luck may still contribute. Defensible reasoning with an unfavorable outcome is a useful loss if the decision was bounded and the learning changes the next move. Weak reasoning with a favorable outcome is a lucky win; do not institutionalize that process. Weak reasoning with a poor outcome requires changing both the product choice and the system."
"Judge the original call from evidence, alternatives, uncertainty, authority, and decision rule available then. Use the result to update what is known now. Do not let the result travel backward in time."

Ask

"Which cell does your organization celebrate too readily? Which cell does it punish too readily?"

Transition

"Now close the loop on the Noted decision."

Slide 17 - Unit 12 individual decision

Time: 14 minutes total: 6 decide, 8 debrief Job: Test honest outcome interpretation and consequential system learning.

Set up the decision

"Separate deploy, exposure, observation, and impact. Compare forecast with result. Identify instrumentation, population, implementation, and attribution limits. Choose continue, expand, pause, rollback, reframe, or stop. Then name one operating-system improvement."

Model debrief

"The capability was deployed, but exposure differed materially across the two partners. The observed overall increase is below the forecast and expansion threshold. Missing actor identity and the governance block weaken attribution and comparability. Durable impact is not established."
"I continue the bounded workflow with Partner A, pause Partner B, and do not expand. I repair actor and meeting-type instrumentation, resolve the permission path, and predeclare the transfer rule for the next partner."
"The original staged decision was defensible because uncertainty, exposure, rollback, and product threshold were explicit. The system failure was treating observability ownership as post-launch work. The change is to require event semantics, coverage, and monitoring ownership at commitment—not at launch."

What strong judgment sounds like

  • Deployment and exposure are not collapsed.
  • The forecast and predeclared rule remain visible.
  • Segment or population differences are not averaged away.
  • Attribution and instrumentation limits change claim scope.
  • Product action and operating-system action are both consequential.

Weak-answer recovery

If a learner says "run it longer":

"Which uncertainty will more time resolve, and which defect requires a design, instrumentation, population, or implementation change instead?"

Transition

"That outcome update completes the four-week Product Decision Case."

Slide 18 - Completed Product Decision Case

Time: 5 minutes Job: Show the capstone as one evolving decision rather than four disconnected artifacts.

Rehearse

"Week 1 bounded the decision and earned the problem. Week 2 matched evidence to the claim and updated the belief. Week 3 chose direction, allocation, sequence, technical option, and ownership. Week 4 made commitment, adaptation, exposure, and learning explicit."
"The case closes the original decision. It does not pretend the product story is finished. The learner should show how judgment changed, what remained uncertain, and which consequence was accepted."
"For a learner without an observed launch outcome, the Week 4 block becomes prospective: exposure stages, forecast, decision rule, instrumentation boundary, anticipated attribution limits, and the system change triggered by missing readiness."

Demo Day standard

"Demo Day is not an artifact showcase and not a build demo. The standard is whether the evolution of judgment is visible and inspectable in six minutes."

Transition

"Here is the six-minute spine."

Slide 19 - Course close and Demo Day handoff

Time: 9 minutes total: 3 synthesize, 6 Q&A Job: Close the course argument and protect the Demo Day format.

Rehearse

"Re-owning the PM core means remaining accountable after the roadmap begins. Present the original decision and why it deserved attention. Show the belief changes, exclusions, trade-offs, dissent, and constraints. Then own the next decision: what the outcome justifies, what remains uncertain, and what changes now."
"You have six minutes to present and four minutes for live feedback. Do not spend the six minutes touring templates. Use the artifacts as evidence behind one narrative of judgment."
"The course does not require a build. A prototype, code, or shipped product can support the case but cannot substitute for the decision chain."

Open Q&A boundary

Use the remaining time to resolve conceptual or Demo Day structure questions. Redirect detailed questions about presentation design, implementation, or tool choice to the weekly check-in.

Final rehearsal line

"The PM core is not owning every task. It is owning the quality, portability, consequence, and learning of the product decision."

Common failure modes and interventions

Failure modeWhat it sounds likeFacilitator intervention
Consensus mistaken for commitment"Sales is not bought in""Do they understand the choice and obligation? Who owns the call?"
Inclusion becomes veto"Security was included, so they decide product scope""Which risk decision is theirs, and which product decision remains with the PM?"
Confidence collapsed"We believe in the opportunity, so commit the date""What effort, dependency, and operational uncertainty must engineering validate?"
Vague executive ask"We need more support""Which decision or resource, from whom, by when, with what consequence?"
Adaptation becomes takeover"I'll run the plan until it is stable""Which interface or right can be repaired instead, and when does control return?"
Fixed review cadence"We always meet daily during launch""Which current consequence requires that frequency?"
Deployment equals exposure"It shipped to two customers""Which eligible users and contexts actually encountered it?"
Average erases population"Overall lift is three points""What differs by workspace, implementation, and eligibility?"
Outcome rewrites decision"The poor result means the strategy was obviously wrong""What was knowable then, and was the decision rule defensible?"
Retrospective without system change"Communicate more next time""Which owner, interface, threshold, or process will materially change?"

    Noted product context: local noted-main repository and wellnoted.dev. All Week 4 stakeholders, dissent, estimates, dependencies, exposure counts, measurements, and outcomes are constructed for practice.

  2. S4-SN-03

    Reforge, Product Leadership, “Awareness, Alignment, Inclusion.” Durable course use: stakeholder groups require different levels of participation based on their contribution and consequence.

  3. S4-SN-04

    Reforge, Product Leadership, “Opinionated Decision-Making.” Durable course use: meaningful inclusion does not require consensus; an accountable product leader must make a choice after input.

  4. S4-SN-06

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Product Conviction” and “Effort and Alignment.” Durable course use: customer-value and impact confidence must be joined by engineering understanding of effort, feasibility, and risk.

  5. S4-SN-09

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Input, Not Oversight,” “Designing Product Reviews,” and “Running Effective Product Reviews.” Durable course use: a review should have a defined input, decision, resolution, or awareness job rather than general approval authority.

  6. S4-SN-10

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Running Team Touchpoints Parts 1 and 2,” plus Product Leadership, “Selective Micromanagement.” Durable course use: vary coordination and intervention with consequence; make increased control purposeful and temporary where possible.

  7. S4-SN-14

    Reforge, Experimentation and Testing, “Test Impact vs. Actual Impact,” “Full vs. Partial Implementation,” and “Alternatives to Holdout Groups.” Durable course use: production population, implementation, novelty, pull-forward, and confounding can make actual impact differ from a winning test.

  8. S4-SN-01

    Reforge, Mastering Product Management, “Empowering Context.” Durable course use: provide deep opportunity, audience, insight, competitive, and success context while avoiding unnecessary implementation prescription.

  9. S4-SN-05

    Reforge, Product Leadership, “Making Clear Asks.” Durable course use: ask executives for an exact decision, input, resource, or support rather than a vague endorsement.

  10. S4-SN-02

    Reforge, Product Leadership, “Narrative, Commitments, Tasks,” and Scaling Product Delivery, “Delivery Systems at Scale.” Durable course use: connect qualitative context, accountable commitments, work, and the wider delivery system.

  11. S4-SN-07

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Fallacy of High-Level Scoping,” “Estimate Effort,” “Sequence Work,” and “Mitigating Risks.” Durable course use: unknowns emerge during execution; update assumptions, dependencies, sequence, and risk controls rather than preserving a false plan.

  12. S4-SN-08

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Delegate and Manage” and “Kick-Off Content.” Durable course use: delegation needs meaningful milestones, ownership, dependencies, and integration context.

  13. S4-SN-11

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Staging Strategies.” Durable course use: launch is not the finish line; staged exposure preserves options and supports post-launch response.

  14. S4-SN-12

    Reforge, Scaling Product Delivery, “Metrics and Instrumentation,” “Communications Plan,” and “Disaster Planning.” Durable course use: define measurement, monitoring, communication, rollback, and response before exposure.

  15. S4-SN-15

    Reforge, Mastering Product Management, “Completing the Decision Loop” and “OKR Reviews and Post-Mortems.” Durable course use: communication, regular review, reinforcement, and reflection close the decision loop and build product intuition.
